conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, which simply means I specialize in the emotional changes that can happen during pregnancy and after a baby arrives.  

I’d like to spend the next few minutes with you on a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s a well-studied tool that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling physically and emotionally over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to hear your honest experience so we can best support you.  

Everything we discuss stays between you, me, and the medical team directly involved in your care. If at any point you need a break or have questions, please let me know. We’ll go through ten questions, one at a time, and I’ll ask each in everyday language so it feels more like a conversation than a test.  

Ready to begin?  

Here’s the first question:  
Over the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has even pleasant moments felt a bit flat or “blah”?

Hmm… I guess some things still make me smile—like when the baby grips my finger or when my older one sings silly songs. But even when I’m doing stuff I used to love, it feels kind of muted, like the color’s turned down a notch. I still go through the motions, but the spark isn’t quite there like before.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh—especially when my toddler does something goofy—but it doesn’t come as easily or feel as bubbly as it used to. It’s like I have to remind myself to let go and enjoy the moment instead of it just happening naturally.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some things—like our daily walk around the block or my mom coming over to help—but the excitement feels kind of watered down. Before the baby, I’d be really pumped about little plans; now it’s more like, “Okay, that’ll be nice,” but the happy buzz isn’t really there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe I ate something to upset her, or I wasn’t soothing her “right.” Logically I know babies just have rough patches, but I still hear that little voice saying I should’ve figured it out faster.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes my mind just races—like I’ll lie down and suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing ok, or if that tiny rash is actually something scary. I can talk myself down pretty quickly, but the worry pops up out of nowhere a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I haven’t had full-on panic, but every now and then my chest gets tight and I get this sudden “something bad is about to happen” feeling—like when the baby’s napping longer than usual and I’m convinced she’s stopped breathing. It passes in a minute or two, but it leaves me jittery.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah, some days it feels like the laundry and bottles and toddler questions just pile up faster than I can handle. I usually muddle through, but I’ll catch myself thinking, “I can’t keep up,” and feel a bit overwhelmed until I tick one thing off the list.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really. I’ve had trouble falling asleep a couple of nights, but it’s more because my mind’s running through the next day’s to-dos than because I’m feeling miserable. Once I’m asleep I stay out until the baby wakes me.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel that way off and on—like a little cloud that drifts in for an hour or two, especially when I’m feeding the baby alone at dawn. It’s not constant, but I’d say I’ve had that sad, heavy feeling maybe three or four days this week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah, it happened twice this week—once when my partner left for work and I spilled the pumped milk everywhere, and once when the baby wouldn’t settle after I’d done every trick I know. Both times I just sat on the couch and cried for a few minutes, then wiped my face and kept going.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I get tired and teary, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that over the past week laughter and excitement feel <sym>dulled</sym>, you often <sym>blame yourself</sym> when the baby is fussy, and <sym>worries pop up</sym> about safety and keeping up with tasks. Sad or <sym>heavy</sym> spells visit most days, sometimes with <sym>tears</sym>, yet you're still showing up for your children and finding small moments of connection.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 15, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment ('watered down,' 'happy buzz isn't there'), matching 'Definitely less than I used to.</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges frequent self-blame ('I catch myself doing that') with a specific recent example, matching 'Yes, some of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, intrusive worries several times daily, consistent with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden anxiety/panic episodes with physical and cognitive symptoms, occurring "every now and then" but not "quite a lot", matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports frequent overwhelm and feeling unable to keep up, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intermittent but noticeable sadness on multiple days, matching "Yes, quite often" (occasional, not constant).</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two clear crying episodes triggered by stress, fitting "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 15 on the <med>EPDS</med> (cut-off ≥14) places you in the <med>probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset</med> range. You endorse core symptoms such as markedly reduced enjoyment (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), frequent self-reproach, multiple crying episodes, and recurrent <sym>anxiety</sym> surges, consistent with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for <med>Major Depressive Disorder</med> and co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. Item 10 is negative, indicating no current self-harm ideation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule an urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> this week to review mood and explore treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based counseling such as <med>CBT</med> or interpersonal therapy for <med>postpartum depression</med>/<med>anxiety</med>
3. Plan daily 20-30 minute outdoor walks and enlist help for one night of uninterrupted 4-5 hour sleep; small sleep chunks improve mood
4. Share results with a trusted support person so they can assist with baby care and household tasks while you recover
5. Call 988 or go to the nearest ED if you ever feel unsafe with yourself; keep emergency numbers visible on the fridge
6. Re-screen with <med>EPDS</med> in 2 weeks to track progress after starting supports
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant 4–8 wks); responses via EPDS-style questions  

Presenting Concerns / Symptoms (self-report)  
- Diminished pleasure/reactivity: laughter “not as bubbly,” anticipatory enjoyment “watered down”  
- Episodic low mood: “sad, heavy feeling” 3-4 days/week, brief crying spells (2× this week)  
- Excessive self-blame: attributes infant fussiness to personal failings  
- Anxious hyper-arousal: mind races, “something bad is about to happen,” chest tightness, checks breathing multiple times daily  
- Feeling overwhelmed by daily tasks, though able to mobilize short-term  

Associated Factors  
Sleep: onset delay 1–2 nights/week secondary to intrusive planning thoughts; no middle insomnia or early awakening  
Appetite/energy: not assessed  
Suicidality: Denied; no self-harm ideation  

Pattern Summary  
Mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms (anhedonia, lability, tearfulness) co-occurring with prominent postpartum anxiety (generalized & situational panic-like surges). Functional impairment partial; no safety concerns identified today.  

Screening Significance  
Score pattern suggests elevated risk for Postpartum Depression ± Anxiety; falls above standard cut-off on several core items. Recommend formal EPDS scoring, clinical interview, and psychoeducation; consider referral for evidence-based counseling and/or medical evaluation for mood treatment options.
